title: Trump Is Losing Touch With the Public
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
One of the few issues that unites voters and politicians of both parties right now is data centers
Three-quarters of Americans would oppose a data center being built near where they live, according to a new poll released last week by Heatmap Pro and Embold Research
The two leading lights of the left, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Bernie Sanders, have sponsored a bill in Congress to create a temporary moratorium on new centers

They have an unlikely ally in archconservative Governor Greg Abbott of Texas, who said yesterday on ABC’s This Week that data-center companies “basically dug their own grave” and “got the backlash they deserve.” Standing against this consensus is Donald Trump

The president remains a big booster of data centers. “Communities that don’t take a data center—they’re making a mistake,” he said Thursday during an interview with his on-again, off-again lackey Michael Cohen. “Data centers throw off tremendous amounts of jobs and money.” This was no one-off

Trump had made several similar comments recently. “If I were the mayor of a town or the governor of a state and I had a chance to get a big plant in, an AI plant or a data center, I would absolutely want it, because the jobs are enormous and the money paid, the taxes paid, are just enormous,” Trump said last week—although he allowed that the sector could use “a little public-relations help.” This puts Trump, the most successful demagogue in American political history, in the unusual position of misreading, and opposing, a populist groundswell
During his 2016 presidential campaign, Trump took many stands that were unpopular among establishment politicians
Some of these positions put him at odds not only with Democrats but also with most Republican elected officials

Trump broke with Republicans in claiming that he would protect social-welfare programs such as Medicare and Social Security, and he broke a bipartisan consensus by attacking free-trade agreements and promising protectionism

On these matters (as well as on his willingness to encourage and participate in gutter racism ), Trump demonstrated that a big constituency existed for views that other politicians had deemed electoral liabilities
Data centers’ political arc has been different
Initially, many officials seemed to back the centers, following exactly Trump’s logic: They offered jobs and tax benefits
But as public opinion turned—driven by a mix of backlash to AI in general, environmental concerns, worries about energy prices, and old-fashioned NIMBYism— politicians changed their view as well

Why has Trump missed the shift? Presumably one reason is that he is surrounded by advisers and tech executives such as David Sacks and Larry Ellison , who are major boosters of and players in the industry

Tech companies invested heavily in Trump at the start of his second administration, lavishing him with gifts, including a gold-plated bauble and donations to projects such as his inauguration and his ballroom, and Trump has reciprocated by taking policy stances that benefit them
Trump may also be personally profiting from the AI boom; his financial disclosures show he’s become more of a tech investor
Trump has always tended to adopt the latest thing he’s heard, no matter what it is
He has been willing to alienate corporate interests in the past—when he saw some political upside
But he is not hearing from voters who might alert him to how unpopular data centers are
Trump’s rallies and speeches once created a feedback loop in which he conveyed his message to voters and—crucially—they conveyed their thoughts to him
Now, as his energy sinks, his travel schedule gets lighter, and security makes events more challenging, Trump is getting out less

Though his stump speeches dragged on for hours, Trump was carefully attuned to audience attention and what did and didn’t work. “You know, if it gets a little boring, if I see people starting to sort of, maybe thinking about leaving, I can sort of tell the audience, I just say, ‘We will build the wall!’ and they go nuts,” he told The New York Times in 2016
I think often about a speech Trump delivered in July 2022
It was billed as the launch of a new policy agenda, but as he read it, both Trump and his audience seemed bored
Then he ad-libbed a riff about trans athletes and the crowd came alive
Trump picked up on the shift and emphasized it; trans issues would become a central talking point for his 2024 campaign
The president has always been susceptible to fake news and bad at filtering information, but rallies provided a gut check about his base, if not about the broader national reality
Now Trump isn’t even receiving that kind of information
One of his major conduits for information is Natalie Harp , a sycophantic aide who isn’t interested in exposing Trump to criticism
He could read public-opinion data, but as his own approval sinks, he has taken to saying (and may well believe) that polls are fake
As his world shrinks, Trump’s populist touch has faded
Despite being elected twice on an antiwar platform, he’s launched attacks on Venezuela and Iran
As the Iran war has gotten bogged down, he’s been incapable of reading the public mood

He has dismissed voter frustration over rising fuel costs, saying “I don’t even think about” gas; he previously called affordability a “hoax.” In response to reports that American sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln were struggling with a long deployment, Trump said they hadn’t been deployed “nearly long enough.” And the collapse of trade talks with Canada on Friday threaten Republican prospects in border states including Michigan and Ohio
Each of these cases represents a growing gap between Trump and his base, but none is as ironic as Trump’s stance on data centers
The AI facilities store terabytes of data, but the president can’t get access to the information about them that he needs

title: Logging in Was Never Supposed to Be This Complicated
excerpt: One afternoon earlier this month, I pulled up to the rec center and realized that I had a problem
body: One afternoon earlier this month, I pulled up to the rec center and realized that I had a problem
It was not the three boisterous tweens in the back seat who were clamoring to be set loose in the basketball gym
I had somehow gotten logged out of Passport Parking, which has become the only way to pay for a spot in much of my town, and it was demanding a four-digit PIN to let me back in
My first guess drew a warning message in red letters: “Invalid PIN

PIN cannot contain 4 sequential numbers, 2 repeated digits, or the last 4 digits of your phone number.” I searched my trusty password manager, which was supposed to spare me these predicaments, but it came up empty
By that point, the kids had run ahead and piled themselves against the gym door, waiting for me to let them in

Lately, the process of accessing apps and websites has grown dizzying. “I’m in password hell,” a colleague confided to me recently. “Every login attempt is playing the lottery.” The problem is not just the sheer number of digital accounts, all of which require their own password, ideally unique and unguessable (which usually also means un-memorizable)
It’s the pileup of solutions to that problem: all of the different layers of software offering to remember your passwords, the six-digit codes sent to your phone, the authenticator apps, the passkeys
Browsers and operating systems compete with third-party password managers to generate, store, and autofill your credentials

Most of my logins live in 1Password, but others are stored in Apple’s Passwords app (usually by accident), and still others were created via “single sign-on” features such as those offered by Google and Facebook
I vaguely recall certain apps—Facebook is one—prompting me many years ago to copy down a set of “login recovery codes” that would become extremely important should I ever get locked out of my account
Whatever device I stored them on was probably wiped and sold long ago
In the 1990s, forgetting your password sometimes meant mailing a po stcard to your service provider and waiting a week or two for it to mail you a new password
In the early 2010s, hackers learned to steal massive troves of logins and then reuse them on other services to steal people’s identities
Things spiraled from there; services started requiring unique, complex passwords with arbitrary requirements

These days, the user experience of logging in is “probably worse than ever,” Troy Hunt, a cybersecurity expert who runs the website Have I Been Pwned, told me. “There’s just no consistency.” Password managers promised a way out, but they often don’t work as seamlessly as you might hope

I click to autofill my password somewhere, and a 1Password authorization appears, only for an iCloud Keychain authorization to pop up directly over it, preventing me from clicking on the 1Password one

When I manually enter a login I thought I remembered, my browser prompts me to remember it; only after I hit “Save” (pro tip: Do not do this) does the website inform me that the password was not recognized

Even when you log in successfully, there’s the tedious dance of waiting for a six-digit authorization code to appear on your phone or in your email, which defeats the concept of a single password for everything
And if you’re somewhere without cell service or you’re sharing a login with someone who isn’t around, you might just be out of luck
At least in theory, each added layer helps prevent hacks and breaches
Erring on the side of safety is worth an amount of inconvenience
At the same time, extra steps can introduce security problems of their own
Last year, Hunt fell for a clever phishing scheme when he clicked a link to log in to his newsletter service
His password manager failed to autofill his information, which should have alerted him that something was wrong, he said
But like the rest of us, he was so used to things not working that he went ahead and manually entered his credentials on a site that turned out to be an impostor, designed to steal and exploit them
None of these obstacles is insurmountable on its own
My problem with Apple’s native password manager fighting with 1Password, for instance, was eventually solved with a 10-minute foray into the bowels of my device settings
But together, they amount to a near-daily irritant
For the less tech-savvy, the situation can be overwhelming

My recent attempts to help my mother fix her password-storage system—which involved loose-leaf notepad sheets full of hand-scrawled credentials scattered around her house like Easter eggs—consumed the better part of a day
By the end, she had all of her credentials updated, validated, and stored in a password manager, just as the experts have been advising for years
But even then, her preferred browser, Google Chrome, showed no interest in surfacing the credentials we had stashed in Apple’s Keychain

And some websites short-circuited her attempts to log in by prompting her to set up a “passkey,” which she interpreted as meaning that her password had failed and she needed to scrap it and set up a new one
Cybersecurity experts will tell you that passkeys—which typically entail logging in to apps or websites with a face or fingerprint scan instead of a password—are the future

When they work properly, they’re both painless and secure. “It may get to a point where we’re all using passkeys and we don’t even know we’re using passkeys,” Lorrie Cranor, a computer-science professor at Carnegie Mellon University who researches privacy and cybersecurity, told me. “I just say ‘Log in’ and I smile at it, and it gets my passkey, and I’m logged in.” But that future isn’t here yet, and in the present, passkeys have added a new layer of frustration
Part of the problem is that virtually no one seems to know what they are. “The fact that even I have trouble explaining them should be a clue,” Cranor said
Her past research on the rollout of two-factor authentication suggests that most people tend to resist new security features for as long as they can
Companies can nudge them, but for websites and apps trying to attract and retain users, pushing people to adopt an unfamiliar authentication technology risks scaring them away
To further complicate matters, passkeys generally aren’t yet replacing passwords altogether, even on sites that use them

title: Where Do America’s Colleges Go From Here?
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts On August 3, Education Secretary Linda McMahon sent a letter to states and higher-e
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts On August 3, Education Secretary Linda McMahon sent a letter to states and higher-education leaders with instructions to, as McMahon put it, “describe to the American public your commitments to rigorous teaching, pathbreaking research, and national service—commitments that make our universities a bedrock institution of the American republic.” A request like that would be simple enough if not for the history between the Trump administration and higher education—a relationship that can fairly be described as antagonistic

Case in point: last year’s “Compact for Academic Excellence in Higher Education,” which critics from across the political spectrum argued effectively asked colleges to compromise academic freedom in exchange for privileged, if vague, access to federal funds
There’s also the suite of federal investigations targeting diversity programs on college campuses

There are outstanding concerns about the experience, the education, and the enterprise of higher education: How much does it cost , and is that more than families can pay ? Who gets in , and why? Are faculty members treated with dignity? What is college even for? So, although college leaders argue that a few of the concerns voiced in the document are legitimate, they also see within it the bane of Ilium . [ Read: A deal that would end universities’ independence ] On this week’s Radio Atlantic, I’m joined by Jack Stripling, the host of the College Matters podcast at The Chronicle of Higher Education , to consider higher education in the Trump era, and the purpose of college itself
I also go back into the Atlantic archives to look at a debate between W
Washington over their theories of advancement for Black people, and how it should inform our thinking about colleges today

The following is a transcript of the episode: Jack Stripling: We keep talking about the politics, but when people are saying I don’t know if college is worth it , they’re usually saying I don’t know if it’s worth the money, not I don’t know if it’s worth risking meeting a liberal person
I’m Adam Harris, and around the country millions of students are getting ready to head back to school, if they’re not already in class
So today, we need to think about education in uncertain times
Now, I was always a big fan of the first day of school
In grade school, I’d pick out my clothes the night before, have them sitting and ready next to my bed
My bag was packed with everything I could possibly need, and some things I definitely didn’t
In college, every new year meant new books, new ideas, and new challenges

But over the last several years, there has been a battle raging for the soul of higher education in America that’s divorced from those idyllic memories—a battle that has many asking what college is supposed to be and whom it is supposed to serve
Earlier this month, Education Secretary Linda McMahon sent a letter to colleges asking them to respond to a series of questions
Questions about their institutions, their programs, and how they contribute to the American project
The letter gives college leaders one more thing to consider in an era marked by funding woes, by fears of enrollment stagnation and decline, technological advancements, and political pressures

How will it all play out? And what will school leaders be thinking about throughout the next year? Jack Stripling is the host of the College Matters podcast at The Chronicle of Higher Education and my former colleague
Stripling: Adam Harris, so good to catch up with you

I want to start with this letter that went out to college leaders recently from Education Secretary Linda McMahon that was effectively the administration’s call to action, right? To prod colleges to address what they see as a sort of outstanding concerns—affordability, viewpoint, diversity, right? That is to say, more acceptable, or more acceptance of conservative views on campus, job preparation, among other things
And it’s sort of been billed as a Compact 2.0, sort of building on the Compact for Academic Excellence in Higher Education that was criticized in 2025
In The Chronicle , you all referred to it as either an olive branch or a gloved fist

So, like, which one is it? How are college presidents viewing this? Stripling: Well, I think that the backstory is important here, Adam, which you know, which is that this is an administration that has essentially been at loggerheads with higher education since day one

The Trump presidency has largely defined its domestic agenda around attacking higher education for its perceived “wokeness.” So this was no surprise that they were going to head in this direction to some extent
They have used, as you know, different types of leverage against all sorts of universities: withholding money, threatening all sorts of things

But the one thing they did do last fall was to release this compact for higher education, which was to say Sign on to these federal priorities and we will, in exchange, give you favorable treatment for federal funding
And I think where it really hurt this administration was college presidents saying, This isn’t even merit-based, and you’re supposed to be the merit people
You’re now saying you’re going to give favoritism to people who agree with you politically
So there was a disconnect between two value systems of the Trump administration
So they end up going back to the drawing board and, as you say, this August 3 letter comes from Secretary Linda McMahon that’s called “a national call to action.” It’s a little softer
It’s more coalition-y , to make a phrase here
It’s based on feedback from influential higher-ed leaders, although some of them seem to be distancing themselves from their role in this
Harris: Wait, how so? Stripling: Well, so, one case in point being the Association of American Universities
So this is the group of high-powered research institutions in this country
It’s an invite-only group; it’s very elite to be a part of it

And they have apparently been working behind the scenes in conversations with the Education Department and with the White House about what they would or wouldn’t want to see in such a letter, but they’ve distanced themselves in saying, Hey, we actually didn’t get to take home drafts
We only had these conversations in person, and some of what we said showed up in there, some of it didn’t

Other people, like the president of Wash U, Andrew Martin, who I think is considered somebody who’s kind of in the “Trump has a point” camp, has said, Hey, I didn’t I didn’t draft this thing, but it does look like some of the things I said are resonating with the Trump administration and ended up in there
But that tells you something about how prickly this is, Adam

So people want to look like they’re playing ball with the Trump administration, but then they have to answer to other constituencies who are deeply skeptical of the motives behind this quote, unquote “agreement” or “value exercise.” Harris: One of the things I noticed as you mentioned is that you had not only liberal groups, academics who might skew a little bit more to the left criticizing this original compact, but you also had conservative think tanks who would say things like At least the previous attempts to change higher education had some sort of legal backing, some sort of legal argument

title: The Atlantic announces Jessica Goldstein as SVP of events
excerpt: The Atlantic has hired Jessica Goldstein as senior vice president of events, who will work in partnership with managing director for events Evan Smith to lead a
body: The Atlantic has hired Jessica Goldstein as senior vice president of events, who will work in partnership with managing director for events Evan Smith to lead and produce the magazine’s robust live programs nationwide
She begins with The Atlantic in early September
Jessica has spent her career telling stories through reporting and creating live experiences that resonate far beyond the stage
She spent eight years creating and leading NPR’s live cultural programming, including creating the Tiny Desk Contest, NPR’s annual search for new musical talent, and the How I Built This Summit
She most recently led the Skoll Foundation’s global convenings strategy and directed the Skoll World Forum
At The Atlantic , she will work with Evan to lead one of the most influential and long-running events practices in media

The Atlantic convenes dozens of annual in-person and virtual events that reach thousands of people every year, anchored by its flagship event, The Atlantic Festival , which returns to New York City September 17–19, after being held for nearly two decades in Washington, D.C
The Atlantic is also under way with a new 50-state tour, The Atlantic Across America , that has already held events in 10 states, addressing some of the most complex issues of our time
Below is Evan Smith’s announcement to staff: I’m excited to let you know that we’ve hired the amazing Jessica Goldstein as our new senior vice president of events

As the second-in-command on our growing team, she’ll oversee the operations, planning, and execution of our robust public programs, working closely with our sales, marketing, design, and CSG colleagues to grow The Atlanti c’s audience and revenue; shine a great, big light on our brand; and—most crucially—bring our journalists and our journalism to stages from coast to coast through The Atlantic Festival, The Atlantic Across America, The Atlantic Summits, and so much more

Jessica comes to us most recently from the Skoll Foundation, where she was managing director of convenings, leading the organization’s global events strategy and directing the Skoll World Forum, a weeklong gathering of heads of state, social entrepreneurs, and civil-society partners
But it’s her reputation at NPR that really precedes her—and makes her the ideal hire in this moment
As senior director and executive producer of Events & Experiential, she spent eight years creating and leading NPR’s live programming, including the Tiny Desk Contest and the How I Built This Summit
Previously she was a senior supervising producer for NPR Music, a senior producer on the science desk, and a producer of audio documentaries known as NPR Radio Expeditions
A native of New York, Jessica is a graduate of the University of Wisconsin at Madison
Jessica believes in the power of storytelling, of sharing ideas and sparking inspiration, which is precisely how we think about our work in the events space
There is no loftier task before us than getting people from divergent backgrounds—great minds who don’t think alike—in a room to listen and talk and continue the conversation after we’re gone
She will bring to bear her decades of experience, her imagination, her creativity, her calm, and her charisma as we expand the ambitious work of the Live team
Press Contacts : Anna Bross and Paul Jackson | press@theatlantic.com

title: A Reverse Ellis Island
excerpt: Photographs by Lisette Poole J ulio Borrell knew he was being deported, but after 47 hours on a bus rattling through Mexico, he still had no idea where the Unit
body: Photographs by Lisette Poole J ulio Borrell knew he was being deported, but after 47 hours on a bus rattling through Mexico, he still had no idea where the United States was sending him
Through the window, he saw the cities give way to sprawling banana plantations and coffee farms

The passengers were still wearing whatever clothes they’d had on when they were detained by ICE: shirts splattered with paint from their most recent job, pajama pants, landscaping-company uniforms, bathing suits
Now he watched as the bus passed a sign for the Guatemala border and then pulled over on the side of the road. “Where are we?” Borrell asked. “Tapachula,” a Mexican immigration agent answered
They were Cuban, Venezuelan, Nicaraguan, and Haitian—many of them elderly, some stripped of their green card after spending most of their life in the United States
The Trump administration, unable or unwilling to send them to their home country, had bused them 2,000 miles, from the U.S. border to a small city where they don’t have legal status

It’s a practice that started last year without any announcement and has quietly grown since then. “Why the hell did they bring us here?” Borrell, who migrated to Miami from Havana in 1980, asked me while I was in Tapachula this month
By the time we met, Borrell, a tall, sinewy 72-year-old with a shock of gray hair, had been in Tapachula for about six months, trying to make enough money fixing tires to rent a studio apartment
He knew that a handful of other Cuban deportees had been flown even farther away, to African nations such as Eswatini and South Sudan
But it was Tapachula that had become a mass waiting area for those rebuffed by U.S. immigration policy, out of sight of lawyers and human-rights defenders
This is now where the largest concentration of deportees is dropped in Mexico, and where most migrants traveling through Latin America en route to the U.S. are halted
Donald Trump can claim that the border is “closed” because it has effectively been relocated to Tapachula

The city looks and feels the way towns in northern Mexico along the U.S. border once did—a dumping ground for those expelled from the United States and a gathering place for those snagged on their way north
Mexican agents pull migrants out of commercial buses and cars on the freeway leaving the city, making sure the deportees don’t attempt to return to the United States
Another set of agents waits for the next busload of Cubans, Venezuelans, and Haitians to arrive so they can be processed
It’s what experts call externalization: the outsourcing of migration management to other countries

Julio Borrell, originally from Cuba, in Tapachula, on July 30, 2026 (Lisette Poole for The Atlantic ) Borrell told me that he’d come to the United States when he was 26 as part of the Mariel boatlift, the mass exodus of Cubans who traveled on crowded boats to Miami in 1980
He had seven American children, 11 grandchildren, and a great-grandchild
He had run a mechanic shop and renewed his visa each time it neared expiration
He could feel his body breaking down after years of physical labor and had been looking forward to retirement and more time with his family in South Florida
Then, last December, he went to his scheduled immigration check-in, as he had done dozens of times before
They sent Borrell to Florida’s Alligator Alcatraz for four months and then to Eloy Detention Center, in Arizona
From there, he was put on a bus for the U.S.-Mexico border and then another, bound for Tapachula
He walked on the side of the road for an hour before borrowing a cellphone to call his family back in Miami. “I’m in some place called Tapachula, Chiapas,” he told his daughter
Borrell, like thousands of other non-Mexicans deported here, arrived without clear legal status and with nowhere to stay
Many deportees sleep on the street for their first few nights

Mexico denies that it is facilitating deportations from the United States to Tapachula, even though more than a dozen migrants described to me the cooperation between U.S. and Mexican immigration agents in their expulsions
According to data from the Mexican Institute for Migration, 12,977 non-Mexicans were deported to Mexico from January 2025 to March 2026, largely to southern Mexico

They joined the tens of thousands of other migrants from all over the world who have been stranded in Tapachula during their journey to the United States, after being blocked by Mexican immigration agents from moving farther north

The mix of nationalities here has prompted officials at the United Nations’ International Organization for Migration to begin informally referring to the city as TapaYork—a kind of reverse Ellis Island
There are roughly 350,000 permanent residents of Tapachula and approximately 60,000 migrants living here

Some have tried to flee Tapachula multiple times, only to be deported back over and over again after being caught by Mexican agents. [ Read: The rushed, blundering effort to send deportees to third countries ] U.S. officials have consistently said that their goal is “zero border crossings”—a more absolutist project than Trump articulated during his first term, when it was easier for migrants to advance beyond Tapachula

This month, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed that his department was accomplishing that goal. (Crossings are indeed way down, but they’re not at zero.) In meetings with their Mexican counterparts, U.S. officials continue to ask for more stringent immigration enforcement and accommodation for long-distance deportations, according to Mexican officials
The Mexicans, who fear unilateral U.S. military action, have generally complied
The Cubans, Venezuelans, and Haitians who are expelled here in buses that typically arrive a few times a week are evidence of Mexico’s acquiescence

In addition to the buses filled with foreigners, Tapachula’s tiny airport sometimes receives as many as five flights of Mexican deportees a day. (There have been more than 196 so far this year.) Most of the Mexicans arriving by plane head straight to the local bus station and return to their home state or to the border again
Some are minors and need to wait for their parents to pick them up

At the Tapachula airport, deportees arrive on flights from the United States. (Lisette Poole for The Atlantic ) In his first weeks here, Borrell, disoriented, was walking to an ATM to see whether he could withdraw cash when he saw a face he recognized
It was a Cuban friend from Miami, who ran a tile business. “What are you doing here, man?” Borrell asked
His friend, who had moved to the U.S. from Cuba when he was 6 and held a green card, had also been deported by bus

title: How to encourage smarter AI use in the classroom
excerpt: This article is from Making AI Work , MIT Technology Review’s limited-run newsletter examining how to apply LLMs across industries
body: This article is from Making AI Work , MIT Technology Review’s limited-run newsletter examining how to apply LLMs across industries
To receive it in your inbox, sign up here
Chatbots took many schools by surprise upon their release a few years ago
Suddenly, students carried an app in their phones that could magically answer almost any homework question or spin up an essay in seconds

Of course, teachers can often tell when a student is using AI—models make mistakes that most humans don’t, and some teachers say that AI-generated text has simple giveaways like too many em dashes .  Nevertheless, the generative AI boom increased the burden on teachers, who were already working long hours to plan lessons, make homework assignments, and grade exams, and now needed to adapt to a new technology
For many, it still feels like there’s no clear path forward

Organizations ranging from OpenAI to UNESCO encourage AI use in the classroom, but many teachers feel confused about how exactly to handle it.  Case study Cheshire Academy is a private boarding and day school in Connecticut with about 400 students in grades 9 through 12
Administrators there don’t force instructors to use AI at all, though the school’s librarian and technology coordinator George Aiello claims the “vast majority” of instructors use it in some way

The educators there are trying a patchwork of programs, including general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT and Perplexity as well as more specialized tools like MagicSchool , an AI-powered platform meant specifically for educators
That patchwork approach is partly because the school, on the advice of consultants, opted to train its staff on general techniques for how to use AI instead of prescribing certain tech

The staff training covered topics like how to craft useful prompts but also stressed the technology’s limits, highlighting its potential for generating incorrect and biased responses.  Now, teachers there often use generative AI to prepare class materials
This means asking the AI of their choice for help with planning lessons or creating grading rubrics
Some even want to use it to help them give feedback to students, though concerns over quality, personalization, and privacy have prevented any of them from doing that just yet
Others, like Miriam Przybyla-Baum, who teaches French, don’t use AI themselves but do address it with their teaching
Przybyla-Baum says she doesn’t really need AI’s help since she’s built up plenty of classroom materials across nearly 30 years of teaching

But she started seeing students try to use AI-powered tools like Google Translate to take shortcuts on their assignments years before ChatGPT’s launch.  She’s developed a system to make students reflect on how AI can and can’t teach language skills
In one assignment, students let a large language model (LLM) edit their homework
Then, they go through the edits and decide which ones were correct and which ones removed their voice
In another, she has students anonymously grade each other’s AI-assisted assignments, making annotations as to which parts they think are AI-assisted
Cheshire Academy is continuing to experiment with how AI can be harnessed productively in the classroom
The school is piloting a program in which students create media and lead discussions regarding healthy AI use
This program, which they call a “Student AI Council,” aims to push students to reflect on how AI should and shouldn’t be used to benefit the community around them
The academy as a whole has since adopted similar techniques to those Przybyla-Baum introduced to make students reflect on their own use of AI
Assignments are now labelled like traffic lights, with green meaning AI is fully allowed and red banning any AI use
Yellow, then, lets the teacher permit some tools while banning the rest, like allowing students to use spell-check but not message a chatbot

The tool As generative AI was becoming mainstream, Cheshire Academy previewed MagicSchool to its staff.  For many, MagicSchool’s main strength seems to lie in the sheer amount of offerings it provides in one package
It can generate questions and assignments of all kinds, from quizzes to worksheets, across many subjects and grade levels
It has a specialized grading rubric generator, which outputs a ready-to-go table that teachers can use to score assignments
It can make presentations and lesson plans and administrative reports, too.  All of this is done through a single platform where educators enter specific prompts tailored for each task

For example, to make an assignment, a teacher can specify the students’ grade level, number of questions, the types of questions (such as multiple choice or short answer), and more, and include documents to align the questions with.  Not every teacher feels comfortable using LLMs to generate student-facing text, whether because they don’t think an AI can produce effective teaching materials or helpful feedback, or because they’re concerned about accuracy
MagicSchool, which has free and paid versions, does offer tools on its platform for other tasks like lesson planning
If teachers want unlimited access and complete records in the system, though, they need to pay just under $100 per year for an individual plan

Alternatively, many of the general-purpose generative AI tools (think the chatbots on offer from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and more) seem suited to administrative tasks, as well, attested by the fact that many of the teachers at Cheshire Academy use those instead
Some of these companies are even rolling out features tailored for schools, to mixed results
How to apply this Meet students where they’re at
Students will be tempted to try AI, and there’s no way to entirely police this for take-home assignments
The internet and social media can spread a lot of misinformation as to what AI can and can’t do, and it’s critical to counter these narratives and teach healthy strategies and relationships
AI is very good at automating tasks, but it struggles with precision and voice
Keep this in mind, especially when generating any text that anyone else may see
Impressionable students who see those in authority using AI in a lazy way could internalize this as an excuse to cut corners in their own work

title: Kids outlearn AI—and we still don’t know why
excerpt: People have been talking to each other for at least 100,000 years, as best we can tell
body: People have been talking to each other for at least 100,000 years, as best we can tell

And in all that time, there has been only one thing in the world that could learn a human language to perfect fluency: a human child.  Now there are two.  Four short years after the release of ChatGPT, many of us now take it for granted that we can converse naturally with our phones or computers
LLMs like Claude, DeepSeek, and OpenAI’s GPT models are fluent and flexible enough to masquerade convincingly as humans
But peek behind the computational curtain, and there’s a catch: Teaching a computer to use human language still requires an inhuman amount of data

An LLM can easily churn through a hundred thousand times more words than a person will experience in the process of mastering their mother tongue—and way more than children might hear by their first birthday, when they typically start to grab hold of language. “The progress recently has been amazing,” Michael C

Frank, a cognitive scientist at Stanford University, says of LLMs. “But we still have to burn down a forest and scrape the entire sum of all human knowledge to re-create this milestone that happens in our living rooms over the course of a year.” This yawning divide between children and machines is called the data efficiency gap

And it raises a tantalizing question for cognitive scientists and a challenge for the architects of AI models: How is it that kids can still outperform the most linguistically sophisticated machines ever built?  Finding answers has stakes for both AI research and cognitive science
For the past decade, language models have mostly gotten better by getting bigger

Meta’s open-weight LLM Llama 3.1, released two years ago, chewed through 15 trillion tokens (word-like chunks of language) in pretraining—the main step of training a model that happens before it is fine-tuned for a specific task, like being a chatbot
Frontier models could be pretraining on 10 times more data, says Ethan Gotlieb Wilcox, a cognitive scientist and linguist at Georgetown University

But there’s only so much internet to train on, and eventually—perhaps as early as the 2030s—the well of easily available data could run dry.  Kids show that it could be possible to learn more with less
A preteen raised in a linguistically rich home may have heard something in the vicinity of 100 million words

Add literacy to the mix and you can boost that word count to maybe 300 million words by age 20.   The difference in scale is something that can only really be gestured at in analogy. “Claude has seen the amount of language that an entire city will experience in one generation,” says Wilcox
If you were to print out on paper all the words used to train a modern LLM, you could make a stack that would reach past the International Space Station
The human preteen’s 100 million words, meanwhile, would stack up just 20 meters

And we can make do with far less than that.  By reverse-engineering the way kids learn, scientists hope to be able to create more data-efficient AI models, which could be useful for everything from training AI effectively on video to creating chatbots that serve minority language communities
Testing hypotheses about human learning in machine models could also settle enduring questions about language and children’s developing minds

Are we born with a language instinct, or would it be possible, even in principle, for a child to learn language purely from experience? Is the way we process language a quirk of our biology, or might at least some of it reflect universal constraints on how languages can be used and learned?  The essential elements Most of us realize language is hard only when we try to learn a new one after childhood

The past perfect tense, rolled r s and nasal vowels, the genitive case, phrasal verbs, grammatically masculine tables and feminine spoons—many are the instruments of linguistic torment for the adult language learner
It’s typically effortless to learn our mother tongues, however

Toddlers usually start producing grammatically correct sentences after hearing something like 10 million words, or 30 million on the high end.  “It’s just totally miraculous,” says Frank. “If you train GPT-2 on 30 million words, you get a nonsense generator; you don’t get a kid.”  Exactly how babies pull this off is a mystery
Researchers know a lot about what kids learn and how they use language at different stages in development, but there’s still a lot we don’t know
Perhaps the most enduring question is why babies can learn language at all

The syntax of human language—the rules for combining words into sentences—includes recursive, nested structures that allow us to express virtually infinite ideas with a finite lexicon of words and pieces of words
This seems like something that should be a problem for babies
They only splash about in the shallows of a fathomless ocean of language
One solution, put forward in the 1950s by the MIT linguist Noam Chomsky, is that babies are born with hardwired knowledge of grammar
Chomsky was reacting to a rival view, championed by the psychologist B.F
Skinner, that language acquisition is entirely environmental
Skinner thought language was learned through conditioning and reinforcement, the way a dog figures out how to sit or shake for treats

Chomsky countered by citing the “poverty of the stimulus”—the idea that language, especially syntax, is too complex and children’s exposure to it too “impoverished” for them to learn entirely from experience. “His signature argument was, essentially, that language cannot be learned on the basis purely of statistics,” says Richard Futrell, a linguist and cognitive scientist at the University of California, Irvine

Instead, Chomsky posited that language is based on a set of logical rules and argued that children needed innate knowledge of those rules to deduce the grammar of their language from scraps of speech. “It’s just totally miraculous … If you train GPT-2 on 30 million words, you get a nonsense generator; you don’t get a kid.” Michael C
Frank, cognitive scientist, Stanford University The Chomskyan view of language dominated linguistics in the US for decades under the moniker of generative grammar

And it was a major influence on computer science in the 1950s and ’60s, when AI was enjoying its first boom time and the lines between linguistics and natural-language processing dissolved in a flood of military funding; the Pentagon wanted computers that could understand English and translate Russian.  Despite early successes of simple neural networks, which learn to recognize and reproduce statistical patterns, AI researchers in the United States largely adopted a rule-based framework influenced by Chomsky’s theories
They tried to teach language to computers by explicitly coding the rules into programs—think less immersion experience, more grammar class
This approach, part of a broader trend called symbolic AI, prevailed for decades
It also largely failed to produce models actually capable of handling human language at scale
Interest in natural-­language processing chilled in the “AI winter” that began in the 1970s.  In the aftermath, neural networks started to make a comeback
But it wasn’t until the 2010s, when computer hardware was getting cheap and capable and the internet was getting big, that their performance began turning heads

By 2018 and 2019, the models BERT and GPT-2, which were built on a new architecture—the transformer—and trained on billions of tokens, made it clear to insiders that learning from a massive glut of data could work for language

title: Legal wrangling over $12.5B Lakers sale shows how family trusts don’t guarantee a business stays in the family
url:
<title>Legal wrangling over $12.5B Lakers sale shows how family trusts don’t guarantee a business stays in the family</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755487/original/file-20260821-50-1r6z0w.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5568%2C3712&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Jeanie Buss is fighting with her siblings over whether to sell their shared stake in the Los Angeles Lakers.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/jeanie-buss-attends-the-los-angeles-premiere-of-netflixs-news-photo/2271580765?adppopup=true">Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The Buss family’s 47-year ownership of the Los Angeles Lakers, 17-time NBA champions, could soon come to an end despite their patriarch’s clear wishes before he died. A group of investors that includes former Disney CEO Bob Iger and Joshua Kushner – the brother of Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law – wants to <a href="https://www.espn.com/nba/story/_/id/49590362/josh-kushner-bob-iger-buy-lakers-12b">buy the basketball team</a> for US$12.5 billion.</p>

<p>The pending deal <a href="https://apnews.com/article/lakers-sale-kushner-iger-12-billion-d5058bb845d87873e23e270a6bb9be9f">would set a record</a>: No other sports franchise has ever fetched that high a price.</p>

<p>After news about the pending sale broke on Aug. 12, 2026, Jeanie Buss, who has run the Lakers since her father, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7519719/2026/08/17/lakers-buss-family-sale-jeanie-governor/">Jerry Buss, died in 2013</a>, said she wasn’t on board. Her five siblings, however, are ready to sell their stakes.</p>

<p>This transaction isn’t only evidence that investors are willing to pay eye-popping sums to buy teams. It also illustrates how hard it was for the late Jerry Buss to structure his estate so that his family could continue to own and run the Lakers for years to come. And it raises <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7527097/2026/08/21/los-angeles-lakers-jeanie-buss-family-sale-legal-expert">a thorny legal question</a>: Who has the authority to sell property held jointly by multiple relatives in a family trust?</p>

<p></p>

<h2>The succession plan</h2>

<p>As <a href="https://www.law.rutgers.edu/bio/weisbord">law professors</a> who study <a href="https://www.law.virginia.edu/faculty/profile/nrc8g/2915359">what happens to property</a> after someone dies, we are fascinated by questions like this because they cast light on the complexities of family dynamics and the challenges that arise when people jointly own unusual assets, such as professional sports teams. </p>

<p>And we’re not alone. Jeanie Buss’ leadership of the Lakers inspired a television series, “<a href="https://www.netflix.com/tudum/articles/running-point-jeanie-buss">Running Point</a>,” starring Kate Hudson. <a href="https://www.netflix.com/tudum/articles/running-point-season-3-news-release-date-cast">Netflix renewed the comedy</a> for a third season in May 2026.</p>

<p>The Buss family has owned the Lakers since Jerry Buss <a href="https://www.nba.com/lakers/history/dr-jerry-buss-the-oral-history-of-the-greatest-owner-in-sports">bought it in 1979</a>. Jerry Buss put the family’s Lakers shares into trusts for his six children.</p>

<p>A trust is a <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/trust">legal arrangement for owning and managing property and other assets</a>. The person who creates the trust must fund it with property and provide instructions to the trustee for how the property should be managed and distributed.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/trustee">Trustees have legal control</a> over property in the trust. <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/beneficiary">Beneficiaries have the right to receive and benefit from the property</a>. You can be both a trustee and a beneficiary of a trust. </p>

<p>Following the succession plan that Jerry Buss reportedly wrote into the family trust, Jeanie Buss became the team’s controlling owner and the Lakers’ “governor” after he died. In the NBA, the governor has the <a href="https://official.nba.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2024/06/NBA-Consitution-By-Laws-June-2024.pdf">final say over a team</a> and represents it to the league. And the NBA’s board of governors has to <a href="https://apnews.com/article/lakers-sale-kushner-iger-12-billion-d5058bb845d87873e23e270a6bb9be9f">approve any team’s sale</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/aug/21/los-angeles-lakers-12-5bn-sale-bob-iger-josh-kushner-private-equity-nba">The Lakers were worth about $1 billion</a> when Jerry Buss died in 2013, and the Buss family owned about two-thirds of the team at the time.</p>



<h2>Most of their stakes already sold</h2>

<p>The Buss siblings <a href="https://www.espn.com/nba/story/_/id/45539931/buss-family-agrees-sell-lakers-mark-walter-sources-say">sold most of their majority stake</a> in the Lakers in 2025 to businessman Mark Walter in a deal that valued the team at $10 billion. But they kept a 17.8% share, and Jeanie Buss was to stay on as <a href="https://sports.yahoo.com/articles/report-mark-walter-tried-loan-034728677.html">governor until 2030</a>.</p>

<p>Walter has now agreed to sell his share to the Iger-Kushner group, although the NBA still needs to approve the deal.</p>

<p>Jeanie Buss’ five siblings reportedly want to sell the family’s remaining stake, but she does not. If the family sells its remaining stake, Jeanie Buss would probably lose her position as the Lakers’ governor because <a href="https://apnews.com/article/los-angeles-lakers-sale-buss-walter-76c25e08bfe36d69c8bb8e0621dd1ead">NBA rules require</a> that a governor hold at least a 15% ownership stake. </p>

<h2>2 sides of the family fight</h2>

<p>Jerry Buss’ six adult children share the team’s financial benefits, but only the trustees have the legal power to manage the property.</p>

<p>Three of the siblings – Jeanie Buss, Janie Buss and Joey Buss – currently serve as co-trustees.</p>

<p>Jeanie Buss’ position appears to rest on conditions written into the trust itself. According to her attorney, <a href="https://www.scribd.com/document/341235859/Buss-Petition">it requires</a> the trustees to do everything possible to ensure that she remain the controlling owner of the Lakers for her lifetime.</p>

<p>That was apparently what their father wanted. In 2017, according to Jeanie Buss’ lawyer, when a prior dispute arose over the trust, a <a href="https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/jeanie-buss-letter-aug-17.pdf">California court reaffirmed</a> that Jeanie Buss remain as controlling owner.</p>

<p>Jeanie Buss’ siblings may counter that the 2017 order does not expressly prohibit a sale and that the trust, according to a prior court filing, permits the trustees <a href="https://www.scribd.com/document/341235859/Buss-Petition">to act by majority vote</a>, which they appear to have done.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.nba.com/lakers/news/mark-walter-acquires-majority-stake-in-lakers">2025 deal struck with Walter</a> also reportedly included a <a href="https://www.legalzoom.com/business-glossary/tag-along-rights">“tag-along” provision</a> that would allow the trust to sell its interest for the same valuation as Walter. The siblings may argue that the currently proposed sale is exactly what was contemplated in the tag-along provision because it exceeds the 2025 valuation.</p>

<p>Ultimately, who prevails will depend on the terms of the trust and the 2025 agreement – neither of which is public – and the 2017 court order.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

<h2>Family feuds over franchises</h2>

<p>Owning a sports team has become a popular asset for billionaires, who <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2025/11/14/collecting-sports-teams-art-cars.html">sometimes see them as a way to strengthen family ties</a>.</p>

<p>The Buss family drama shows that sharing ownership of a professional sports team can instead cause family disputes that play out publicly. One heir might prefer to remain actively involved in managing it, while the others may want to sell their stakes.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2021/07/16/sports/football/denver-broncos-sale-bowlen.html">Denver Broncos</a> were controlled by a family trust until 2022. The family sold the football team because the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2022/06/08/sports/football/denver-broncos-walton-penner-family-auction-sale.html">siblings could not agree</a> on which of them would otherwise own it.</p>

<p>Another dispute involving the <a href="https://abcnews.com/Sports/sources-pistons-owner-tom-gores-set-buy-stake/story?id=114300796">Los Angeles Chargers</a> arose in 2021 when one sibling, who served as co-trustee, sought to force a sale of the family trust’s stake in the football team, while her brother and other siblings sought to preserve family control.</p>

<p>A similar trust dispute cropped up in 2022 over family ownership of the <a href="https://www.espn.com/mlb/story/_/id/34071306/orioles-ceo-john-angelos-wrested-control-team-expense-brother-suit-claims">Baltimore Orioles</a>, when one of the owner’s sons sued the other over control of the trust and the baseball franchise, including whether to sell the team.</p>

<p>These cases underscore an important lesson for estate planning: Giving several heirs equal shares of an estate does not mean that they will amicably decide how to manage the property they own together.</p>

<h2>Sibling disputes aren’t unusual</h2>

<p><a href="https://finred.usalearning.gov/Planning/ConsiderTrusts">Anyone can establish a trust</a>, and disputes over trusts usually have nothing to do with professional sports.</p>

<p>One of us (Weisbord) worked with two colleagues on a <a href="https://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6294318">study of trust lawsuits</a> filed in California that will be published in September 2026. It found that in 25% of those 640 cases, siblings were fighting each other in court.</p>

<p>Conflicts when parents do what Jerry Buss did by naming some of his children as both trustees and beneficiaries, but leaving others with beneficiary status only, were the most common type of dispute.</p>

<p>For the Buss family, the question of what happens to its trust could decide whether a basketball dynasty ends.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290114/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Jeanie Buss is fighting with her siblings over whether to sell their shared stake in the Los Angeles Lakers

Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic via Getty Images The Buss family’s 47-year ownership of the Los Angeles Lakers, 17-time NBA champions, could soon come to an end despite their patriarch’s clear wishes before he died

A group of investors that includes former Disney CEO Bob Iger and Joshua Kushner – the brother of Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law – wants to buy the basketball team for US$12.5 billion
The pending deal would set a record : No other sports franchise has ever fetched that high a price
After news about the pending sale broke on Aug. 12, 2026, Jeanie Buss, who has run the Lakers since her father, Jerry Buss, died in 2013 , said she wasn’t on board
Her five siblings, however, are ready to sell their stakes
This transaction isn’t only evidence that investors are willing to pay eye-popping sums to buy teams
It also illustrates how hard it was for the late Jerry Buss to structure his estate so that his family could continue to own and run the Lakers for years to come

And it raises a thorny legal question : Who has the authority to sell property held jointly by multiple relatives in a family trust? The succession plan As law professors who study what happens to property after someone dies, we are fascinated by questions like this because they cast light on the complexities of family dynamics and the challenges that arise when people jointly own unusual assets, such as professional sports teams
Jeanie Buss’ leadership of the Lakers inspired a television series, “ Running Point ,” starring Kate Hudson
Netflix renewed the comedy for a third season in May 2026
The Buss family has owned the Lakers since Jerry Buss bought it in 1979
Jerry Buss put the family’s Lakers shares into trusts for his six children
A trust is a legal arrangement for owning and managing property and other assets
The person who creates the trust must fund it with property and provide instructions to the trustee for how the property should be managed and distributed
Trustees have legal control over property in the trust
Beneficiaries have the right to receive and benefit from the property
You can be both a trustee and a beneficiary of a trust
Following the succession plan that Jerry Buss reportedly wrote into the family trust, Jeanie Buss became the team’s controlling owner and the Lakers’ “governor” after he died
In the NBA, the governor has the final say over a team and represents it to the league
And the NBA’s board of governors has to approve any team’s sale
The Lakers were worth about $1 billion when Jerry Buss died in 2013, and the Buss family owned about two-thirds of the team at the time
Most of their stakes already sold The Buss siblings sold most of their majority stake in the Lakers in 2025 to businessman Mark Walter in a deal that valued the team at $10 billion
But they kept a 17.8% share, and Jeanie Buss was to stay on as governor until 2030
Walter has now agreed to sell his share to the Iger-Kushner group, although the NBA still needs to approve the deal
Jeanie Buss’ five siblings reportedly want to sell the family’s remaining stake, but she does not

If the family sells its remaining stake, Jeanie Buss would probably lose her position as the Lakers’ governor because NBA rules require that a governor hold at least a 15% ownership stake. 2 sides of the family fight Jerry Buss’ six adult children share the team’s financial benefits, but only the trustees have the legal power to manage the property
Three of the siblings – Jeanie Buss, Janie Buss and Joey Buss – currently serve as co-trustees
Jeanie Buss’ position appears to rest on conditions written into the trust itself
According to her attorney, it requires the trustees to do everything possible to ensure that she remain the controlling owner of the Lakers for her lifetime
That was apparently what their father wanted
In 2017, according to Jeanie Buss’ lawyer, when a prior dispute arose over the trust, a California court reaffirmed that Jeanie Buss remain as controlling owner

Jeanie Buss’ siblings may counter that the 2017 order does not expressly prohibit a sale and that the trust, according to a prior court filing, permits the trustees to act by majority vote , which they appear to have done
The 2025 deal struck with Walter also reportedly included a “tag-along” provision that would allow the trust to sell its interest for the same valuation as Walter
The siblings may argue that the currently proposed sale is exactly what was contemplated in the tag-along provision because it exceeds the 2025 valuation
Ultimately, who prevails will depend on the terms of the trust and the 2025 agreement – neither of which is public – and the 2017 court order

title: Many Americans are moving away from congregations, but not necessarily from religion – movies, plays, art and social media fill the gap
url:
<title>Many Americans are moving away from congregations, but not necessarily from religion – movies, plays, art and social media fill the gap</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755421/original/file-20260821-50-gm39cr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C16%2C1024%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Theatergoers arrive for &#39;Leopoldstadt,&#39; a play about several generations of a Jewish family in Vienna, at Wyndham&#39;s Theatre in London in 2020.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.es/detail/fotograf%C3%ADa-de-noticias/theatre-goers-arrive-for-an-evening-show-of-fotograf%C3%ADa-de-noticias/1207190032?adppopup=true">Isabel Infantes/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>“Emma,” a young Jewish woman who we met in 2019, didn’t belong to a synagogue. She didn’t have a Jewish partner. She didn’t observe Jewish rituals regularly. On most surveys about religion, she would not seem very engaged with Judaism.</p>

<p>But as Emma talked about what she did in her free time, a very different picture began to emerge. She visited Jewish websites and enjoyed listening to Jewish music. She read books about Jewish topics and had recently attended a retreat for young Jewish adults to learn Torah while also doing yoga.</p>

<p>She was highly invested in learning about Judaism, but she explored her identity without joining traditional institutions. </p>

<p>Most major surveys about religion ask whether someone belongs to a congregation, <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religious-landscape-study/">how often they attend services</a>, whether they pray regularly and whether belief is important in their lives. Those measures help identify broad shifts, like the growing percentage of <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2024/01/24/religious-nones-in-america-who-they-are-and-what-they-believe/">Americans who are religiously unaffiliated</a>: the “nones.”</p>

<p>But many Americans’ religious lives, like Emma’s, are not disappearing; they are <a href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/702572/americans-religious-engagement-holds-lower-levels.aspx">moving away from membership of traditional institutions</a>. To understand what religion looks like in 21st-century America, researchers may need to ask different questions. </p>

<h2>Learning through art</h2>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=fe8whmsAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">As scholars of Judaism</a> <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=5xbfH4oAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">and education</a>, we have been exploring how people learn about religion beyond traditional places like synagogues, Jewish schools and summer camps. Between 2019 and early 2023, <a href="https://nyupress.org/9781479838561/judaism-mediated/">we spoke with hundreds of people</a> and explored different leisure time activities to discover what people learn about Judaism and Jewishness through cultural arts. </p>

<p>We interviewed dozens of audience members at Jewish-themed shows on Broadway, <a href="https://www.newyorktheatreguide.com/theatre-news/news/everything-you-need-to-know-about-leopoldstadt-on-broadway">such as “Leopoldstadt”</a> <a href="https://www.newyorktheatreguide.com/show/26500-parade">and “Parade.”</a> We attended Jewish concerts and asked attendees what they learned. We explored how social media communities offer spaces to talk about different Jewish topics, like what fans learned about ultra-Orthodox Judaism from watching <a href="https://www.imdb.com/title/tt3069894/">the television show “Shtisel</a>.”</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/_lMpx_QM7x8?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">‘Shtisel,’ an Israeli series about an ultra-Orthodox family in Jerusalem, ran for three seasons.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Our research revealed that there is a vibrant ecosystem of people learning about religion in their leisure time. Through the arts, both Jews and non-Jews encounter Jewish history, Jewish religious practices and representations of Jewish communities.</p>

<h2>Screen and stage</h2>

<p>Most people we spoke with told us that they felt meaningful connections to Judaism during activities that would rarely appear on a standard religion survey.</p>

<p>“Joan,” an unmarried woman in her 50s from Connecticut, told us that she was deeply invested in Judaism, but felt that synagogues and Jewish community centers were not welcoming to single people without families. Instead of joining a Jewish institution, she watched Jewish-themed TV shows and movies on Netflix, and joined social media communities to chat with other fans. </p>

<p>“Luis,” who lived in Boston but was born in Argentina, was <a href="https://theconversation.com/fiddler-on-the-roof-may-be-many-americans-image-of-judaism-but-american-jews-heritage-is-stunningly-diverse-229170">a Sephardic Jew</a>, a group that traces their ancestry and traditions to Jewish communities who once lived in Spain and Portugal. His wife was Ashkenazi, meaning her ancestors <a href="https://www.myjewishlearning.com/article/sephardic-ashkenazic-mizrahi-jews-jewish-ethnic-diversity/">came from Central and Eastern Europe</a>. She considered herself secular, and so the couple joined the <a href="https://www.circle.org/">Worker’s Circle</a>, a nonreligious Ashkenazi institution rather than a synagogue.</p>

<p>Yet Luis loved deepening his knowledge of Sephardic culture, and he often attended concerts of music in Ladino, <a href="https://theconversation.com/on-passover-some-sephardic-jews-revisit-not-only-the-story-of-their-ancestors-but-also-their-ladino-language-278290">a Sephardic language related to Spanish</a>, with other Sephardic immigrants.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/MrS2uNeUxiA?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">American singer Sarah Aroeste writes and performs in Ladino.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>For Joan and Luis, these activities were not peripheral to their Jewish lives. Rather, they were <a href="https://nyupress.org/9781479838561/judaism-mediated/">central avenues for learning and community</a>. We interviewed hundreds of Jews who told us that cultural experiences were opportunities to reflect on Jewish practices, explore questions of belonging, connect with family histories and find friends with common interests.</p>

<h2>New questions</h2>

<p>Some aspects of these patterns were distinctive to Judaism. Historically, many Jews have understood Judaism to be <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2021/05/11/jewish-identity-and-belief/">a cultural world</a>, and not only a theological tradition. Learning about cultural dimensions of Judaism <a href="https://nyupress.org/9781479822287/jewish-sunday-schools/">has long been part of Jewish education</a>.</p>

<p>The broader phenomenon of informal learning, though, extended far beyond a single tradition. Across America, increasing numbers of people learn about religion through media, cultural productions and digital networks. Christians may study biblical themes through podcasts, online discussion groups <a href="https://apnews.com/article/christian-influencers-girls-gone-bible-megan-ashley-1241a2e0e54fc9fb828734ea911dd77d">or religious influencers</a>. Muslims may participate in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-26376-8_5">online learning communities</a> that connect believers across the world. </p>

<p>The challenge for religion researchers, then, is not simply to determine whether engagement with religion is rising or falling. Rather, it is to develop more nuanced ways of understanding how people explore religious themes and practices, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2023/06/21/opinion/religion-dechurching.html">beyond traditional institutions</a>. Only then can we more fully understand how contemporary Americans actually live their religious lives.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289940/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
