<title>Most Westerners know Buddhism through meditation, but everyday Buddhist life looks quite different in Thai temples</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/755014/original/file-20260819-50-jcqdtb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5760%2C3840&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Buddhist daily practice in Thailand involves many rituals.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/faithful-in-the-south-vihara-wat-pho-wat-phra-royalty-free-image/764777955?phrase=thai%20laymen%20%20Buddhist%20ritual&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Catherine Leblanc/Godong/Stone via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>I recently returned from leading an educational <a href="https://www.retreatours.com/thailand2026/">program in Thailand</a> focusing on how Buddhists practice the religion in their day-to-day lives. The participants – Buddhist practitioners from North America and Europe – wanted to deepen their understanding and practice of the religion.</p>

<p>Many Western Buddhists’ practices centers on meditation. As a <a href="https://www.rhodes.edu/bio/brooke-schedneck">scholar of contemporary Thai Buddhism</a>, I have taught many students and adults in the U.S. who have a similar understanding. </p>

<p>Although meditation can be very important to many practitioners, as I show in my 2023 book, “<a href="https://www.shambhala.com/living-theravada-9781611809718.html?srsltid=AfmBOooYvIioXyY83cGUCpNf9hznYHqFs0jFLJXvrrcBn2HY3468pXQ1">Living Theravada</a>,” Buddhism is more than an intellectual tradition focused on the mind. In countries with a majority Buddhist population, such as Thailand, Buddhist practice involves rituals, offerings to monks and visits to temples, among others traditions.</p>

<p>Here are three ways in which Buddhism shapes daily life in Thailand.</p>

<h2>1. Merit-making</h2>

<p>A central part of daily practice is performing rituals associated with merit-making. To make merit means to do something morally good that will generate good karma – actions that are believed to impact this life and future ones. The simplest way to do this is to make a monetary donation to a temple. </p>

<p>There are often several merit-making activities in temples that are meant to be fun and engage participants. For example, one can place a small sheet of gold leaf on a part of a Buddha statue where one would like help or healing, such as one’s mouth if someone often uses their voice for their work or the ankle where they would like help or healing.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754834/original/file-20260819-50-h74tfd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A woman in a blue shirt places a small sheet of gold leaf on a golden Buddha statue." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754834/original/file-20260819-50-h74tfd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754834/original/file-20260819-50-h74tfd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754834/original/file-20260819-50-h74tfd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754834/original/file-20260819-50-h74tfd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754834/original/file-20260819-50-h74tfd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754834/original/file-20260819-50-h74tfd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754834/original/file-20260819-50-h74tfd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Buddhists believe that placing a sheet of gold leaf on the statue of a Buddha will help in healing.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/asian-woman-to-pray-respect-to-buddha-statue-in-royalty-free-image/2162788488?phrase=Putting%20Gold%20Leaf%20On%20Buddha%20Statue&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Prapass Pulsub/Moment via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Another fun activity is ritually purifying the “chedi,” or a large monument that enshrines sacred relics. Thai Buddhists fill a container with blessed water, which is attached to a pulley that leads to the upper part of the chedi. The container empties when it reaches the top, and participants make merit by symbolically cleansing the sacred monument. </p>

<p>Making offerings to specific <a href="https://www.dharmathai.com/birthday-buddhas/">Buddha statues</a> representing the different <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/1061855">zodiac signs</a> based on one’s day and year of birth is common. In Thai temples, one can often find eight Buddha statues in a row, all in different poses; each represents a day of the week, with Wednesday being divided into morning and evening. Those born on a Friday, for example, will make an offering to the Buddha statue corresponding to their day of birth. </p>

<p>Worshipers can also make merit by directing donations to the zodiac animal associated with their birth year. Those born during the year of the monkey can place a flag or paper decorated with the monkey symbol on or around a sacred structure inside the temple hall. In other words, individuals can make merit connected to their own circumstances, relationships and aspirations, while practicing generosity. </p>

<h2>2. Spiritual connections with monks</h2>



<p>A foundational feature of Theravada Buddhism is the relationship between monastics and the lay people. This relationship is a delicate balance where laity offer alms while the monks offer spiritual wisdom and guidance. As monks’ lives are dedicated to Buddhism, they are believed to accrue much merit, <a href="https://www.globalbuddhism.org/article/view/1269">which Buddhists believe they can then transfer</a> to people who make offerings.</p>

<p>However, there are times when these bonds can be tested. During COVID-19, for example, <a href="https://tricycle.org/article/thai-monks-covid-reflection/">the laity did not go into the temples</a> for fear of contracting the virus. This made it difficult for monks to obtain food and maintain connections with their local Buddhist community.</p>

<p>The laity’s faith in monks and in their ability to <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/trans-trans-regional-and-national-studies-of-southeast-asia/article/abs/everyday-scandals-regulating-the-buddhist-monastic-body-in-thai-media/6B0FE2EB1995CD741C0139042E086E43">provide merit and moral guidance can suffer</a> if monks break their vows, such as by drinking alcohol or having sex. In 2022, for example, <a href="https://therevealer.org/sex-scandals-and-buddhist-monks-in-thailand/">a well-known monk</a> was found to have had an affair with a model. Thai Buddhists felt disappointed and raised questions about the ability of young monks to take their vow of celibacy seriously. </p>

<h2>3. Rituals and wish-making</h2>

<p>The ultimate goal of Buddhist practitioners is enlightenment, or nirvana – freedom from the cycle of birth and death and suffering. But most Buddhists see this goal as out of reach in this lifetime and instead have <a href="https://tricycle.org/article/thai-wish-making/">desires for worldly things</a>, such as getting a job, winning the lottery or finding a spouse. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754667/original/file-20260818-50-li3398.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A large statue of the elephant-headed god Ganesha with a silver umbrella above it and two mouse statues nearby, in the courtyard of a temple with colorful red walls." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754667/original/file-20260818-50-li3398.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754667/original/file-20260818-50-li3398.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=413&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754667/original/file-20260818-50-li3398.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=413&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754667/original/file-20260818-50-li3398.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=413&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754667/original/file-20260818-50-li3398.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=519&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754667/original/file-20260818-50-li3398.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=519&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754667/original/file-20260818-50-li3398.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=519&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A statue of the Hindu god Ganesha at the entrance to the Wat Sri Suphan temple in Chiang Mai, Thailand.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/wat-sri-suphan-chiang-mai-thailand-royalty-free-image/900465178?phrase=thailand%20buddhist%20%20temples%20ganesha&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">© Marco Bottigelli/Moment via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Thai Buddhist temples often have icons of Hindu gods, such as <a href="https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/special-reports/2515699/behold-the-exam-results-god">Ganesha</a> and <a href="https://www.bangkokpost.com/thailand/general/2399270/erawan-shrine-donations-hit-b1-8bn">Brahma</a>, who are believed to grant these worldly wishes. Some temples may also have shrines dedicated to indigenous gods or spirits of the land. Since these gods are believed to be concerned with worldly success, they are popular places where people pray for wealth, job promotion, romance or fertility. </p>

<p>These rituals involve an exchange, where worshipers <a href="https://www.nationthailand.com/thailand/general/40022564">promise to return</a> with certain objects the god or spirit is believed to enjoy, such as hard-boiled eggs, figurines of elephants or flower garlands, if their wish comes true. </p>

<p>Buddhism in Thailand is embedded into everyday lives and collective concerns. At the end of 10 days, my program participants learned the value of merit-making and felt benefit from performing rituals. They saw how Buddhism extends beyond the individual pursuit of mental transformation through meditation.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289681/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Fish DNA in Ozark streams reveals region’s complex geologic history</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754908/original/file-20260819-50-3bfonp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C168%2C4032%2C2688&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A student collects a water sample for DNA analysis.</span> <span class="attribution"><span class="source">David Duvernell</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>My students and I encountered a mystery. We were partnering with the Missouri Department of Conservation to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/edn3.510">monitor for fish presence and abundance</a> in the Missouri Ozarks. We visited half a dozen rivers and streams across the region and collected a few cups of water from each.</p>

<p>We were testing for <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gecco.2019.e00547">DNA in the environment</a> to determine which species had left behind their genetic material and were therefore <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2025.124531">present in the stream</a>. There was no need to capture or even see the species themselves. We were delighted to detect a variety of species in their appropriate habitats that are <a href="https://mdc.mo.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/2026%20SOCC%20Checklist.pdf">considered at risk in Missouri</a>, including the <a href="https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/lake-sturgeon">lake sturgeon</a>, <a href="https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/crystal-darter">crystal darter</a> and <a href="https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/alabama-shad">Alabama shad</a>. In the surface waters emerging from one large underground spring, we detected DNA from a <a href="https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/salem-plateau-cavefish">cave-dwelling fish species</a> that would never have been detected by researchers who caught or looked only for fish in the surface waters.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/wY_AiXN4QNY?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            
          </figure>

<p>But there was a problem: We were certain we would find one particular species in every stream: the <a href="https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/bleeding-shiner">bleeding shiner</a> (<em>Luxilus zonatus</em>), one of the most common fish in Ozark streams. To have confidence in our results we needed to understand why the bleeding shiner DNA did not show up in every sample, as we had expected. We checked our sampling technique, our water chemistry and other aspects of our testing. </p>

<p>In the data itself, we found a clue: The streams in which we detected bleeding shiner DNA all drained to the southern Ozarks, and the streams in which bleeding shiner DNA was not detected were all in the northern Ozarks. We could draw a line through the north-south drainage divide between those areas.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754380/original/file-20260817-50-31fro8.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A small fish with silver scales, a dark midline stripe and a dark crescent-shaped bar at the gill opening." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754380/original/file-20260817-50-31fro8.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754380/original/file-20260817-50-31fro8.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=391&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754380/original/file-20260817-50-31fro8.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=391&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754380/original/file-20260817-50-31fro8.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=391&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754380/original/file-20260817-50-31fro8.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=492&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754380/original/file-20260817-50-31fro8.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=492&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754380/original/file-20260817-50-31fro8.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=492&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">A bleeding shiner swims above a grassy bottom.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/bleeding-shiner">Cliff White/Missouri Department of Conservation</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>An ancient artifact</h2>

<p>Some follow-up sleuthing revealed something we hadn’t known at the start: Northern Ozark bleeding shiners <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/fishes10090443">have a different DNA history</a> from their southern relatives, even though the fish look identical and are, in fact, the same scientific species.</p>

<p>To human observers, the Ozarks can seem a relatively continuous landscape. For fishes, however, that landscape is divided into a series of separate drainage networks. Streams may arise only a few miles apart yet flow in opposite directions, ultimately connecting to entirely different river systems with distinct geologic histories.</p>

<p>Hundreds of thousands of years ago, the ancestors of northern populations interbred with another species of shiner, leaving behind a genetic signature of ancient hybridization that survives today, but only in certain drainages. Though they look the same, and were in rivers humans view as neighboring, these fish had distinctly different genetic histories.</p>

<p>We had been looking for just one DNA signature, assuming that all bleeding shiners would share that identity. Environmental DNA analyses like this can sometimes turn up <a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genbank/">unknown or unidentifiable sequences of DNA</a>. When we looked more closely at those results, we were able to identify which previously unknown sequence corresponded to the northern populations of bleeding shiner.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754381/original/file-20260817-60-sgzyu6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A small fish swims above a rocky stream bottom." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754381/original/file-20260817-60-sgzyu6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754381/original/file-20260817-60-sgzyu6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=449&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754381/original/file-20260817-60-sgzyu6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=449&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754381/original/file-20260817-60-sgzyu6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=449&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754381/original/file-20260817-60-sgzyu6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=565&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754381/original/file-20260817-60-sgzyu6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=565&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754381/original/file-20260817-60-sgzyu6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=565&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The bleeding shiner is common throughout waterways in the Missouri Ozarks.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bleeding_Shiner.jpg">Wabeggs/Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Geologic history</h2>

<p>Our findings were a concrete illustration that today’s rivers are products of ancient landscapes. During the glacial advances of the Pleistocene epoch – from about 2.5 million to about 12,000 years ago – some rivers repeatedly changed course. </p>

<p>Streams that are isolated today were once connected. Others that share a common geography and are ecologically quite similar today may have had entirely separate histories. The species that exist in rivers and streams today are the products of those <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1095-8649.2010.02769.x">long and complicated geological and evolutionary processes</a>. </p>

<p>Specifically in Ozark streams, northern drainages that flow into the Missouri and Mississippi rivers were <a href="https://www.missourigeologists.org/EarlierGuidebooks/Guidebook1998-Part2.pdf">directly influenced by glacial advances</a> that molded, modified, wiped out and recreated drainage connections and patterns of flow across the landscape.</p>

<p>In contrast, the southern Ozarks drainages were relatively isolated from disruptive glacial advances. South-flowing drainages, such as the St. Francis, Black, White and Spring rivers, contain <a href="https://archive.org/details/fishesofmissouri0000will">more endemic species</a> and genetically unique populations. Examples include the genetically distinct Black River walleye and numerous minnows, sunfishes and darter species that are unique to specific streams.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

<p>This project reminded my students and me that biodiversity monitoring by sampling DNA in the environment doesn’t just reveal what species are present.</p>

<p>The water samples we took contained records of the ancient landscapes that shaped those species. Every sample of river water is more than an inventory of life – it’s a window into the evolutionary history of an entire watershed.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289351/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

David Duvernell , CC BY My students and I encountered a mystery
We were partnering with the Missouri Department of Conservation to monitor for fish presence and abundance in the Missouri Ozarks
We visited half a dozen rivers and streams across the region and collected a few cups of water from each
We were testing for DNA in the environment to determine which species had left behind their genetic material and were therefore present in the stream
There was no need to capture or even see the species themselves
We were delighted to detect a variety of species in their appropriate habitats that are considered at risk in Missouri , including the lake sturgeon , crystal darter and Alabama shad

In the surface waters emerging from one large underground spring, we detected DNA from a cave-dwelling fish species that would never have been detected by researchers who caught or looked only for fish in the surface waters
But there was a problem: We were certain we would find one particular species in every stream: the bleeding shiner ( Luxilus zonatus ), one of the most common fish in Ozark streams
To have confidence in our results we needed to understand why the bleeding shiner DNA did not show up in every sample, as we had expected
We checked our sampling technique, our water chemistry and other aspects of our testing

In the data itself, we found a clue: The streams in which we detected bleeding shiner DNA all drained to the southern Ozarks, and the streams in which bleeding shiner DNA was not detected were all in the northern Ozarks
We could draw a line through the north-south drainage divide between those areas
A bleeding shiner swims above a grassy bottom

Cliff White/Missouri Department of Conservation An ancient artifact Some follow-up sleuthing revealed something we hadn’t known at the start: Northern Ozark bleeding shiners have a different DNA history from their southern relatives, even though the fish look identical and are, in fact, the same scientific species
To human observers, the Ozarks can seem a relatively continuous landscape
For fishes, however, that landscape is divided into a series of separate drainage networks
Streams may arise only a few miles apart yet flow in opposite directions, ultimately connecting to entirely different river systems with distinct geologic histories

Hundreds of thousands of years ago, the ancestors of northern populations interbred with another species of shiner, leaving behind a genetic signature of ancient hybridization that survives today, but only in certain drainages
Though they look the same, and were in rivers humans view as neighboring, these fish had distinctly different genetic histories
We had been looking for just one DNA signature, assuming that all bleeding shiners would share that identity
Environmental DNA analyses like this can sometimes turn up unknown or unidentifiable sequences of DNA
When we looked more closely at those results, we were able to identify which previously unknown sequence corresponded to the northern populations of bleeding shiner
The bleeding shiner is common throughout waterways in the Missouri Ozarks
Wabeggs/Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA Geologic history Our findings were a concrete illustration that today’s rivers are products of ancient landscapes
During the glacial advances of the Pleistocene epoch – from about 2.5 million to about 12,000 years ago – some rivers repeatedly changed course
Streams that are isolated today were once connected
Others that share a common geography and are ecologically quite similar today may have had entirely separate histories
The species that exist in rivers and streams today are the products of those long and complicated geological and evolutionary processes

Specifically in Ozark streams, northern drainages that flow into the Missouri and Mississippi rivers were directly influenced by glacial advances that molded, modified, wiped out and recreated drainage connections and patterns of flow across the landscape
In contrast, the southern Ozarks drainages were relatively isolated from disruptive glacial advances
Francis, Black, White and Spring rivers, contain more endemic species and genetically unique populations
Examples include the genetically distinct Black River walleye and numerous minnows, sunfishes and darter species that are unique to specific streams

<blockquote>
<p><strong>How do ice cubes cool a drink? – Helen, age 12, Boston, Massachusetts</strong></p>
</blockquote>

<hr>

<p>I like to make my own iced tea. First, I steep about a quart of terrifically strong hot tea and pour it into a pitcher loosely filled with ice cubes straight from the freezer. The result is about two quarts of delicious, cold tea, with a few ice cubes floating on top.</p>

<p>What’s the science behind my perfect pitcher of iced tea? A simple answer is that the near-boiling tea transferred its hotness to the below-freezing ice cubes. This transfer raised the temperature of the ice cubes so that much of the ice melted. That both cooled the tea to a refreshing drinking temperature and diluted it for a proper taste.</p>

<p>My iced tea process reminds me of <a href="https://picryl.com/media/microgravity-39f9e8">physics experiments</a> I worked on that flew on the space shuttle Columbia in the 1990s. I was interested in how liquids turn into solids in the absence of gravity. </p>

<p>Both those space experiments and the making of iced tea depend on liquids or solids getting hotter or colder in just the right combination. The explanation for how it all works depends on two related concepts: temperature and energy.</p>

<h2>What are temperature and energy?</h2>

<p>The concept of temperature grew out of the sense of what feels hot and cold to human touch. Boiling water is too hot to touch safely, and a candle flame is even hotter. Ice cubes feel cold. A thermometer is a special hotness meter that more reliably and repeatably determines the degree of hotness or coldness of substances than our sense of touch.</p>

<p>Eighteenth-century physicist <a href="https://www.britannica.com/biography/Daniel-Gabriel-Fahrenheit">Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit</a> defined the point when ice melts or water freezes as 32 degrees of temperature – what we we now call 32 degrees Fahrenheit in his honor. He also defined the temperature at which water boils and turns into steam to be 212 degrees F.</p>

<p>Energy is a more complicated concept. One way to think about energy is as a way to track what it costs nature to makes changes from one set of conditions to another. There are many types of energy. Thermal energy is related to temperature. Kinetic energy is based on how fast stuff is moving. Other forms of energy include, to name only a few, electromagnetic energy, chemical energy and nuclear energy.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753708/original/file-20260812-60-v5ni1j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A grid of blue circles featuring flames, solar panels, a lightbulb, a beaker, a nuclear icon, an electrical plug, an apple tree, and a hammer with nails are used to describe different types of energy." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753708/original/file-20260812-60-v5ni1j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753708/original/file-20260812-60-v5ni1j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=415&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753708/original/file-20260812-60-v5ni1j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=415&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753708/original/file-20260812-60-v5ni1j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=415&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753708/original/file-20260812-60-v5ni1j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=521&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753708/original/file-20260812-60-v5ni1j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=521&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753708/original/file-20260812-60-v5ni1j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=521&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Physicists point to many types of energy.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/illustration/types-of-energy-diagram-royalty-free-illustration/1430197096?phrase=types%20of%20energy%20libguides&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;slot=2&amp;adppopup=true">blueringmedia/iStock via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Another type of energy is called <a href="https://www.britannica.com/science/potential-energy">potential energy</a> and it accounts for the energy stored by the forces acting between or within objects. It is those forces that control the transfers from one type of energy to another. Examples of potential energy that you can see are a rubber band stretched and about to snap back or a boulder sitting at the top of an incline, ready to roll. On a microscopic level, potential energy is composed of all the interacting forces between the atoms and molecules that make matter.</p>

<p>Once a boulder begins to roll down the hill, its potential energy from the force of gravity first transforms to kinetic energy and then maybe to thermal energy or to the work of knocking down a tree. Although energy can transform from one type to another, the total amount of energy always remains the same. Whatever amount of energy is gained in one place must be lost from somewhere else. Scientists call this rule of nature <a href="https://www.britannica.com/science/conservation-of-energy">conservation of energy</a>, or in cases involving thermal energy, the <a href="https://www.britannica.com/science/first-law-of-thermodynamics">first law of thermodynamics</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753714/original/file-20260812-50-r47qvo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A hiker pushes a large boulder balancing on top of a rocky hill." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753714/original/file-20260812-50-r47qvo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753714/original/file-20260812-50-r47qvo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753714/original/file-20260812-50-r47qvo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753714/original/file-20260812-50-r47qvo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753714/original/file-20260812-50-r47qvo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753714/original/file-20260812-50-r47qvo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753714/original/file-20260812-50-r47qvo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Once this boulder rolls down the hill, its potential energy will transform to kinetic energy.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/young-girl-making-an-effort-to-push-a-big-stone-on-royalty-free-image/1448284658?phrase=person%20pushing%20a%20boulder&amp;slot=2&amp;adppopup=true">Paul Biris/Moment via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>On a molecular level</h2>

<p>As an example of the distinction between energy and temperature, compare a cup of hot tea and an iceberg. The hot tea is clearly at a much higher temperature than the iceberg, but the large iceberg has vastly more energy than the tiny cup of tea.</p>

<p>The tea is hotter than the iceberg because the molecules that make up the tea are moving faster than the molecules that make up the iceberg. The temperature is essentially the average energy of the molecular movements.</p>

<p>The speed and energy of a typical single liquid molecule are greater than for a typical single iceberg molecule. But the iceberg has many, many more molecules, all moving around, interacting with each other and transferring vast amounts of energy between their <a href="https://openstax.org/books/college-physics/pages/14-3-phase-change-and-latent-heat">kinetic and potential energies</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753709/original/file-20260812-50-w30vw8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A large iceberg sits in the middle of a large body of water. A ship emitting a plume of smoke can be seen in the distance." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753709/original/file-20260812-50-w30vw8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753709/original/file-20260812-50-w30vw8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=343&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753709/original/file-20260812-50-w30vw8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=343&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753709/original/file-20260812-50-w30vw8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=343&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753709/original/file-20260812-50-w30vw8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=431&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753709/original/file-20260812-50-w30vw8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=431&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753709/original/file-20260812-50-w30vw8.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=431&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">Picture a tiny cup of tea aboard a ship compared to a humongous, looming iceberg. Which has more energy?</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/just-in-from-long-ice-patrol-the-coast-guard-cutter-modoc-news-photo/515561442?adppopup=true">Bettmann via Google Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The trick is energy transfer</h2>

<p>Back to the question of making iced tea. When the hot tea encounters the ice cubes, the molecules of tea-flavored water collide with the molecules on the surface of the ice. The liquid’s molecules slow down. The ice’s molecules speed up, and some even leave the solid and mix in with the liquid tea.</p>

<p>The tea loses thermal energy and lowers its temperature. That <a href="https://phet.colorado.edu/sims/html/energy-forms-and-changes/latest/energy-forms-and-changes_all.html">energy transfers</a> to the ice, which gains that energy and increases its temperature.</p>

<p>The process of energy moving from one place to another due to differences in temperature is called heat transfer. Left to itself, nature transfers thermal energy only from higher to lower temperatures. That observation is called the <a href="https://www.britannica.com/science/second-law-of-thermodynamics">second law of thermodynamics</a>. It’s why you will never see a cup of cold tea turn into a cup of ice cubes and hot tea.                 </p>

<p>In my pitcher, this process continues until the ice eventually reaches a temperature of 32 degrees F, its melting temperature. At that point, the ice cannot take any more energy and stay solid, even though it is still absorbing thermal energy from the hotter tea. Instead, any additional thermal energy absorbed by the 32 degrees F ice transforms it into 32 degrees F water.</p>

<p>Heat transfer cooling means that energy leaves the tea. Conservation of energy means a matching amount of energy raises the temperature of the ice to 32 degrees F and then turns some of that ice into 32 degrees F water. Thus the thermal energy of the tea turns into the potential energy of the water molecules that used to be part of the ice, lowering the temperature of the liquid in the pitcher. The process continues until eventually all the tea and whatever ice that survived the melting are at the same refreshing 32 degrees F.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753713/original/file-20260812-50-zthhek.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A hand grips a clear glass of orange liquid with ice, featuring a slice of lemon on the rim and a red curly straw." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753713/original/file-20260812-50-zthhek.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753713/original/file-20260812-50-zthhek.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753713/original/file-20260812-50-zthhek.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753713/original/file-20260812-50-zthhek.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753713/original/file-20260812-50-zthhek.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753713/original/file-20260812-50-zthhek.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753713/original/file-20260812-50-zthhek.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Cheers to a tasty, cool drink!</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/hand-holding-refreshing-lemon-drink-with-straw-in-royalty-free-image/2242591490?adppopup=true">Pablo Jeffs Munizaga - Fototrekking/Moment via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>

<p>Keep all this in mind as you enjoy your ice-cold drink on a hot summer day. Don’t dawdle, though, as the air temperature in the room or your warm hand on the glass can transfer their thermal energy to melt the rest of the ice and then begin to raise the temperature of your drink!</p>

Vollmann has spent his career refusing to distill the world into dichotomies.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/william-t-vollmann-attends-the-letterature-rome-news-photo/1534912849?slot=50&amp;adppopup=true">Maria Moratti/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>With forecasters of doom <a href="https://trevoraleo.substack.com/p/three-theses-on-the-literacy-crisis">debating the end of reading</a>, of publishing <a href="https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/2026/08/reading-crisis-postliterate-age/687618/">and of literacy in general</a>, what should we make of William T. Vollmann’s forthcoming novel, “<a href="https://www.skyhorsepublishing.com/arcade-publishing/9781648211881/a-table-for-fortune-box-set/">A Table for Fortune</a>”?</p>

<p>Spanning four volumes at 3,000 pages, is it madness? A determined attempt to silence print’s naysayers?</p>

<p>I have been writing about Vollmann’s works since I penned the introduction to “<a href="https://udpress.udel.edu/book-title/william-t-vollmann-a-critical-companion/">William T. Vollmann: A Critical Companion</a>” more than 10 years ago. </p>

<p>The 67-year-old author has spent his career going big, in every sense, and I would not be the first to describe his approach to his art <a href="https://newrepublic.com/article/118748/william-t-vollmanns-dangerously-uncorrupted-literary-mind">as uncompromising</a>. </p>

<p>His projects grapple with weighty matters such as <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2007/03/18/books/review/Kirn.t.html">global poverty</a>, <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/series/BR3/seven-dreams/">the history of North America</a> and <a href="https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2018/10/william-vollmann-carbon-ideologies/568309/">climate change</a>. Few of his roughly 25 books run under 500 pages. About half try to keep his readers engaged for several hundred beyond that. Many of them supplement the text with photographs, epigraphs, glossaries, family trees, sketches, timelines, variant tables of contents, alternating fonts and notes to the reader. The essay “<a href="https://www.mcsweeneys.net/articles/an-oral-history-of-william-vollmanns-rising-up-and-rising-down">Rising Up and Rising Down</a>,” his philosophical and journalistic inquiry into the nature of violence, clocks in at over 3,000 pages across seven volumes. </p>

<p>But to those who might argue that this is the worst time to put a monster of a novel into print since <a href="https://www.lindahall.org/about/news/scientist-of-the-day/johannes-gutenberg/">the days before Johannes Gutenberg created</a>  the movable-type printing press in the 15th century, I would say that Vollmann’s approach is needed now more than ever.</p>

<h2>The ‘poisoned harvest’ of 9/11</h2>

<p>After reading Vollmann’s works and occasionally speaking with him in person or via post, I join others in being powerfully struck by his unrivaled intelligence, empathy and work ethic. His books are not big for the sake of being big. They reflect the deep sense of responsibility he feels toward his subjects.</p>

<figure class="align-right ">

VOLLMANN,' wrapping around the edges." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753373/original/file-20260811-70-d7whcf.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753373/original/file-20260811-70-d7whcf.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=789&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753373/original/file-20260811-70-d7whcf.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=789&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753373/original/file-20260811-70-d7whcf.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=789&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753373/original/file-20260811-70-d7whcf.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=991&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753373/original/file-20260811-70-d7whcf.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=991&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753373/original/file-20260811-70-d7whcf.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=991&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">‘A Table for Fortune’ explores what happens when the response to the horrors of 9/11 becomes an arena for perpetration of further crimes.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://skyhorse-us.imgix.net/covers/9781648212086.jpg?auto=format&amp;w=298">Skyhorse Publishing</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In the case of “A Table for Fortune,” that subject is, as Vollmann declares in the opening volume, the cause and effects of 9/11 – “tracing the roots of that crime in one direction and its poisoned harvest in another.” </p>

<p>It is a novel of ideas and a novel of feelings, the former expressed in the tale of a CIA man who bears the code name DAVE, and the latter the purview of his son, Matthew. DAVE is a brilliant, deeply committed Cold War analyst whose faith in America’s mission gradually erodes after 9/11 and <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/european-journal-of-international-security/article/what-the-war-on-terror-leaves-behind-an-introduction/6815F9E0BB023A2FEB68D54F560899B2">the ensuing war on terror</a>. Matthew, by contrast, is less interested in geopolitics but just as invested in questions about the nature of America. His desire for purpose in life is deeply informed by a notion that the nation still harbors opportunities for freedom. At the same time, his search for that freedom leads him into such dangers as homelessness and addiction.</p>

<p>The book will be published at a challenging moment for Vollmann — and for reading more broadly.</p>

<p>In 2022 alone, he lost his daughter, was <a href="https://harpers.org/archive/2023/11/four-men/">dropped by Viking</a>, his longtime publisher, and the <a href="https://bigreaderbadgrades.substack.com/p/we-always-leave-things-unfinished">supporters of his archives</a> at Ohio State, and got <a href="https://www.metropolitanreview.org/p/the-last-contract">hit by a car</a> while crossing a street. He has also been fighting an incurable case of colon cancer, racing against the clock to see a few final projects to completion.</p>

<p>Meanwhile, the nation’s educational system is constantly having to <a href="https://static1.squarespace.com/static/589c9a6be6f2e10ec8f0b764/t/62e480ac2af198075148954f/1659142318613/Among+many+U.S.+children%2C+reading+for+fun+has+become+less+common+_+Pew+Research+Center.pdf">calibrate its expectations for reading down</a>, and publishers find themselves confronting <a href="https://news.ufl.edu/2025/08/reading-for-pleasure-study/">steadily worsening odds</a> that the average reader will even pick up a book in the next year. </p>

<p>To the extent that there is a reading public, they’re assumed to be increasingly ill-equipped to handle the very sorts of things <a href="https://metropolitanreview.com/the-last-contract/">that motivated Viking to drop Vollmann</a>: His books seem too long, too complex and too expensive to publish.</p>

<h2>Deep dives can confront shallow duplicity</h2>

<p>But I think the apparent gulf between Vollmann’s work and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2025.113288">America’s dismal reading data</a> could be thought of differently. What if the challenging complexity and political engagement of his tomes are exactly what’s needed? </p>

<p>Today, <a href="https://philarchive.org/archive/VACEOT">fact and fantasy intermingle freely</a> as a consequence of political scheming and jockeying for economic advantage. Political discourse is reduced to opinions <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/jcmc/zmab002">at once homogenous and balkanized</a>, reinforced by <a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691175515/republic?srsltid=AfmBOoqdIai-jDarAQbbVJQ_p6K8bS1eR3wVGvd3gDl374XYMmr32nDv">the echo chambers of the day’s regnant algorithms</a>. Then there are the fragmented attention spans birthed by our dearly beloved screens, which cultivate a kind of cognitive whiplash that <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/science/2022/jan/02/attention-span-focus-screens-apps-smartphones-social-media">vacillates between amnesia and yearning for more</a>.</p>

<p>It’s easy to become dispirited and cynical: The field seems too big, and the game rewrites the rules too quickly for anyone to figure out how to overcome these forces. </p>

<p>Maybe the first step is recognition.</p>

<p>What happens, Vollmann’s works ask, when serving the good is revealed as its opposite? What happens when the response to the horror of 9/11 becomes an arena for perpetration of further crimes, rather than the healing of wounds already inflicted? </p>

<p>Even as the invasion of Afghanistan in 2001 and of Iraq in 2003 became <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2021/09/02/two-decades-later-the-enduring-legacy-of-9-11/">largely condoned</a> by the American public, displacement, suffering and impasse persist in the region, now in the form of the ongoing conflicts in the Gaza Strip and Iran. The broader post-9/11 strategy seems directed <a href="https://www.damemagazine.com/2026/03/24/what-the-war-on-terror-built/">against stable governance</a> in the Middle East generally.  </p>

<p>Whether one works for the CIA – as do several of Vollmann’s central characters in “A Table for Fortune” – or occupies a less central node in the networks of power, it is not hard to recognize that the best intentions can be perverted, that one’s idealistic labor may unknowingly be lent to furthering the cloaked ambitions of the wicked. </p>

<p>Such legacies of 9/11 are the sort of uncomfortable and powerful matters to which Vollmann directs attention. And if people are to grapple with such thorny topics, they need to be delineated in detail and at length, as they are in “A Table for Fortune.” </p>

<p>A work like this is not only a book about powerful conspirators. It is also a book that can help keep people afloat as they navigate the tumultuous seas of the post-truth era, dodge the whirlpools of digital banality and resist the leviathans of techno-capitalism.</p>

<h2>Literary life rafts</h2>

<p>Vollmann is not going it alone. Far from it. </p>

<p>He follows the tradition of what scholars call “<a href="https://read.dukeupress.edu/comparative-literature/article-abstract/64/3/241/7718/The-Maximalist-Novel?redirectedFrom=fulltext">literary maximalism</a>” – works that are ambitious in scale and scope, containing narratives flush with surprising intersections, proliferations and divergences.</p>

<p>His works build on such earlier mega-novels as Thomas Pynchon’s “<a href="https://thomaspynchon.com/pynchon-cover-art/gravitys-rainbow/">Gravity’s Rainbow</a>,” William Gaddis’ “<a href="https://www.nyrb.com/products/the-recognitions">The Recognitions</a>” and John Barth’s “<a href="https://archive.org/details/sotweedfactor006326mbp/page/n7/mode/2up">The Sot-Weed Factor</a>,” which together confront the complexities of America’s past and present. Their topics include the limits of authenticity and how to grasp understanding in a world awash in deceit. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Black-and-white photo of middle-aged man standing in snowy woods, holding a cigarette." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754131/original/file-20260814-50-epx63y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754131/original/file-20260814-50-epx63y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=401&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754131/original/file-20260814-50-epx63y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=401&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754131/original/file-20260814-50-epx63y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=401&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754131/original/file-20260814-50-epx63y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=504&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754131/original/file-20260814-50-epx63y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=504&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754131/original/file-20260814-50-epx63y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=504&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/writer-william-gaddis-on-january-25-1968-in-new-york-new-news-photo/462477049?slot=1&amp;adppopup=true">Santi Visalli/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Vollmann also joins ambitious contemporaries such as David Foster Wallace, whose “<a href="https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/david-foster-wallace/infinite-jest/9780316920049/?lens=little-brown">Infinite Jest</a>” interrogates the loss of self to entertainment and the vapid slogans of popular culture.</p>

<p>Behind each is arguably the grandest American novel of all, “<a href="https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2701">Moby-Dick</a>.” </p>

<p>I was not surprised to learn that Vollmann <a href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/voyage-french-polynesia-herman-melville-course-write-moby-dick-180972525/">visited Polynesia</a> in 2019 to walk in Herman Melville’s footsteps. Melville, after all, was wracked by difficulties that should never have been his to bear: constant problems with publishers, uncomprehending reviews, <a href="https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/1982/05/10/melvilles-withdrawal">endlessly faltering finances</a> and the loss of a teenage son <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1943-278X.1976.tb00881.x">to a self-inflicted gunshot wound</a> that may not have been an accident.</p>

<p>In other words, Vollmann’s work is not entirely an outlier. Neither is his readership.</p>

<p>Indie publishing houses like Deep Vellum are celebrating thick books, and not just those from American authors. Mircea Cărtărescu’s 2015 “Solenoid,” which begins with a fictional biography set in Cold War Romania, has earned <a href="https://thebookerprizes.com/the-booker-library/features/mircea-cartarescu-and-sean-cotter-interview-solenoid">a dedicated following</a> in translation. Michael Lentz’s “Schattenfroh,” a 1,001-page novel that follows the internal narrative of a tortured subject confronting centuries of history, likewise <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/07/books/review/michael-lentz-schattenfroh.html">garnered considerable attention</a> when its English translation dropped in 2025.</p>

<p>In his note to the reader, Vollmann explains that the ongoing failures most strikingly signaled by 9/11 are matters of “lessons not learned,” “expediencies of power” and “consciences disabled,” in addition to that most cunning arbiter: “chance.”</p>

<p>The same list of conditions is relevant to the debates about our faltering literacy. If, as seems likely, “A Table for Fortune” is one of Vollmann’s final books, it crowns a career that reminds readers that the world’s troubles must be apprehended as much more complex than a few data points and alarmist sound bites suggest. </p>

<p>Indeed, books like “A Table for Fortune” may be among the most essential tools for keeping our heads above water.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/288326/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Trump blows up the US-Canada relationship
excerpt: President Donald Trump at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, on August 21, 2026. | Win McNamee/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newslet
body: President Donald Trump at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, on August 21, 2026. | Win McNamee/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada is back in full force.  What’s happening? Remember last week, when Trump said that the US and Canada had a trade deal in place? It turns out they do not

After negotiations fell through on Friday, Trump responded with a 50 percent tariff on some $20 billion in Canadian goods, plus threats of higher tariffs on cars, car parts, and steel to come in 2027.  Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and other administration officials are also leaning into ever more inflammatory rhetoric, with Vance taunting Canada on Monday as “a state” that “quite literally would get invaded by a foreign country were it not for the umbrella of protection provided by the United States of America.”  How is Canada responding? With outrage, as my colleague Caitlin Dewey explains , and with tariffs of their own: On Saturday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that his country would match US tariffs “dollar for dollar,” starting early next month.  “We cannot accept what the U.S. has offered,” he wrote, “and we will not give what they have asked.” In addition to trade terms, the US allegedly made requests to weaken Canada’s French-language protections, which Carney said would have infringed on Canadian “sovereignty.” Why does this matter? Immediately speaking, tariffs make things more expensive at a time when voters are already incensed over prices and the Iran war is making inflation worse ; their impact could be especially felt in border states like Maine and Michigan, which also happen to have high-stakes, closely contested Senate races coming up in 72 days.  On a longer timeline, the Trump administration is doing damage to the US-Canada relationship that goes far deeper than specific tariffs and will be far harder to reverse
Already, in January, Carney delivered a speech charting a plan to move past relying on the US as a global partner; Trump’s latest trade war will only accelerate that rupture

And with that, it’s time to log off… Violent crime rates in the US are falling across the board , according to new 2025 statistics released by the FBI, including the murder rate, which just hit a 70-year low — tied for the lowest ever recorded
That’s good news in any context, but if you want to learn more, my colleague Bryan Walsh took a crack at explaining how it happened
You can read his article here with a gift link.  Thanks for reading, have a great evening, and we’ll see you back here tomorrow!

title: The view from a very angry Canada
excerpt: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney (right) and Dominic LeBlanc, the minister responsible for Canada-US trade, arrive at a press conference in Ottawa, Ontario o
body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney (right) and Dominic LeBlanc, the minister responsible for Canada-US trade, arrive at a press conference in Ottawa, Ontario on August 22, 2026. | Dave Chan/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day

President Donald Trump is putting the “war” in “trade war.” Or so his senior officials really want you to believe. “At dawn begins an economic D-Day,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wrote Sunday night, previewing the latest round of sanctions against Iran.  “It’s a country that doesn’t have a military,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said , incorrectly, of Canada over the weekend. “To think that they’re going to go to war with Donald Trump and actually win that war…is foolish.” The war with Iran is literal, of course

But in both cases, the Trump administration is trying to weaponize America’s economic might to get its way in otherwise stalled negotiations.  Iran and the US have been locked in on-again, off-again talks for almost the entire six months since the US-Israeli strikes began

And last week, trade negotiations between the US and Canada collapsed amid disputes over tariffs on key Canadian industries, as well as US demands that Canada weaken protections for its culture and the French language
Now, both countries are promising steep retaliatory tariffs on goods ranging from cars and steel to anoraks.  Trump is betting that economic pain will produce the concessions diplomacy hasn’t
But Americans also suffer the fallout from these kinds of tactics.  Go a little deeper View Link I am one such American

Hello! Bonjour! I am planning to visit Montreal over Labor Day weekend…and have begun to fear that my New York plates might provoke some patriotic ne’er-do-well to key my car.  As someone who grew up on the Canadian border, with Canadian friends and Canadian radio stations and Canadian flags on most every pole, the notion that I might be newly unwelcome — or, quelle horreur, despised — in Canada is a new and unpleasant one

Not to fear, said my colleague Zack Beauchamp. (Zack lives 90 minutes northwest of me in Ontario, and is Vox’s go-to expert on Canadian concerns.) Most Canadians “are actually quite chill toward individual Americans,” he said, and he therefore rates it “unlikely” that anyone will vandalize my vehicle.  At the same time, Zack said, most Americans fail to realize how dramatically, and perhaps permanently, Canadians have turned on the US as a country
To many of us, the trade war is a tedious or incomprehensible policy dispute
To Canadians, it’s seen as a real threat to their sovereignty.  Zack shared this example from his own family, which — existential stakes notwithstanding — kind of cracked me up
His wife, who is Canadian, is participating in a popular boycott movement and has “shifted literally everything she purchases” to avoid American products
That includes buying terrible Canadian-made dishwasher pods whose wrapping doesn’t dissolve in the machine

Or purchasing him a deodorant from the puzzlingly named brand Green Beaver, which is “somewhat worse at repelling smell,” Zack said.  “Whenever I ask her about why she does these things, she points to those World War II posters about reducing gas use — carpooling so you aren’t riding with Hitler ,” Zack said. “Because that is literally how Canadians think about these things: as a war for their survival.” The rupture is existential for Americans, too, I think — albeit in a different and less urgent way

It has to do with what American identity represents in the world today.  That’s more abstract than something like the cost of a car (which, by the way, will likely rise dramatically if Trump implements the tariffs he threatened this morning on Truth Social)
But the way the world sees America also matters
A new study found that raising cage-free hens generates more greenhouse gas emissions than conventional egg farming

If you don’t want to choose between animal welfare and climate change…may we suggest switching your eggs out for tofu or beans ? (Sorry, sorry! But not every tip in this newsletter can be uplifting.) Before you go… Did you know… that researchers believe young children’s brains don’t record permanent memories because they’re busy prioritizing other patterns and skills? It’s a phenomenon called “infantile amnesia,” and we’re still a long way from fully understanding it.  Today’s trivia: What’s the traditional, three-letter nickname for students and graduates of Yale? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Last week we asked you for the insect stage after the larva
That would be the pupa or pupal stage — basically, insect adolescence.

title: This transplant surgery could save countless lives. Why aren’t we doing more of them?
excerpt: Physicians perform a kidney transplant. | BSIP/Universal Images Group via Getty Images In an episode from the fifth season of Grey’s Anatomy , Miranda Bailey, p
body: Physicians perform a kidney transplant. | BSIP/Universal Images Group via Getty Images In an episode from the fifth season of Grey’s Anatomy , Miranda Bailey, played by Chandra Wilson, orchestrates an ambitious 12-person paired kidney transplant surgery
Six living donors each give one of their kidneys to a stranger and six recipients receive one in return

While the show, which is still on the air almost 18 years later, often blurs the line between fact and fiction, this particular form of kidney transplant, called a paired kidney exchange chain, has become increasingly common in the United States
Key takeaways Kidneys and livers, two organs that a living donor can donate, account for more than 90 percent of the demand on the US organ waiting list

More living liver donors could help close a critical gap, just as they did for kidneys.  We currently don’t have systems in place, such as a national registry, to implement a strong living donor liver transplant system.  New organ preservation technology, universal protections for living donors, and broader surgical training could help us change that
Rewatching the show (sue me), I wondered if such donation chains are viable for other organs (or tissues ) that can be donated by living donors
The liver, the only organ that can regenerate itself over a span of six to eight weeks, struck me as a particularly notable candidate
As with any surgical procedure, donating part of one carries some risk, but in most cases a person can safely continue to lead a healthy life afterward
And the need for them far exceeds what deceased donors can provide
Right now, there are more than 100,000 people on the waitlist for organs

Over the past decade, using organs from living donors to meet organ demand has emerged as a particularly effective strategy.  In 2025, around 24 percent of kidney transplants used living donors, according to preliminary data from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN), the public-private partnership responsible for maintaining equitable organ allocation policies

Infrastructural advances, such as the establishment of the National Kidney Registry (NKR) in 2007, have helped reduce wait time for kidneys, provided financial support for donors, and facilitated close to 11,000 paired exchange kidney transplants
In a paired exchange, two patients who each have a willing but incompatible organ donor simply swap donors — my donor gives to you, yours gives to me
Ultimately, both of us receive a kidney that our bodies are more likely to accept

By contrast, only about 6 percent of the roughly 12,000 liver transplants performed in the US last year used living donors.
